claim: PTEN is the second most commonly deleted gene in cancer.
source: The tumor suppressor gene PTEN is the second most commonly deleted gene in cancer.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself, but is presented as established knowledge.

claim: PTEN deletions often include portions of the chromosome 10q23 locus beyond the bounds of PTEN itself, which frequently disrupts adjacent genes.
source: Such deletions often include portions of the chromosome 10q23 locus beyond the bounds of PTEN itself, which frequently disrupts adjacent genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by genomic data analysis shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ATAD1 directly and specifically extracts the pro-apoptotic protein BIM from mitochondria to inactivate it.
source: ATAD1 directly and specifically extracts the pro-apoptotic protein BIM from mitochondria to inactivate it.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro extraction assays shown in Figure 2I-K and co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D-E.

claim: Cultured cells and mouse xenografts lacking ATAD1 are hypersensitive to clinically used proteasome inhibitors.
source: Cultured cells and mouse xenografts lacking ATAD1 are hypersensitive to clinically used proteasome inhibitors, which activate BIM and trigger apoptosis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by viability assays in Figure 3A-D and xenograft experiments in Figure 4A-B.

claim: PTEN is deleted in more than 33% of metastatic prostate tumors.
source: The tumor suppressor gene PTEN is deleted in more than 33% of metastatic prostate tumors and nearly 10% of glioblastoma multiforme and melanoma (Worby and Dixon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Worby and Dixon, 2014.

claim: PTEN is deleted in nearly 10% of glioblastoma multiforme and melanoma.
source: The tumor suppressor gene PTEN is deleted in more than 33% of metastatic prostate tumors and nearly 10% of glioblastoma multiforme and melanoma (Worby and Dixon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Worby and Dixon, 2014.

claim: Collateral deletion of neighboring genes along with tumor suppressor genes can generate context-dependent vulnerabilities specific to tumor cells.
source: Prior research has demonstrated that the 'collateral' deletion of neighboring genes along with tumor suppressor genes can generate context-dependent vulnerabilities specific to tumor cells (Muller et al., 2015; Kryukov et al., 2016; Mavrakis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to three prior studies.

claim: ATAD1 is located only 40 kb upstream of PTEN.
source: Only 40 kb upstream of PTEN is ATAD1, which encodes a AAA+ ATPase involved in protein homeostasis on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) (Chen et al., 2014; Okreglak and Walter, 2014; Nakai et al., 1993; Wang and Walter, 2020; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: ATAD1 encodes a AAA+ ATPase involved in protein homeostasis on the outer mitochondrial membrane.
source: Only 40 kb upstream of PTEN is ATAD1, which encodes a AAA+ ATPase involved in protein homeostasis on the outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) (Chen et al., 2014; Okreglak and Walter, 2014; Nakai et al., 1993; Wang and Walter, 2020; Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: ATAD1 hydrolyzes ATP to directly remove substrate proteins from the OMM.
source: ATAD1 hydrolyzes ATP to directly remove substrate proteins from the OMM (Wang and Walter, 2020; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: ATAD1 appears particularly suited to extract tail-anchored (TA) proteins, which harbor a C-terminal, single-pass transmembrane domain.
source: ATAD1 appears particularly suited to extract tail-anchored (TA) proteins, which harbor a C-terminal, single-pass transmembrane domain.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about ATAD1 function and is supported by the in vitro extraction assays in Figure 2.

claim: The absence of ATAD1 leads to the accumulation of TA proteins on the OMM and significant mitochondrial dysfunction.
source: In contexts unrelated to cancer, it has been shown that the absence of ATAD1 leads to the accumulation of TA proteins on the OMM and significant mitochondrial dysfunction (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2014.

claim: ATAD1 is essential for life in mammals.
source: This housekeeping role of ATAD1 is important for cellular health, as evidenced by the findings that ATAD1 is essential for life in mammals and has been conserved over the 1 billion years of evolution separating yeast and humans (Zhang et al., 2011; Ahrens-Nicklas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2011 and Ahrens-Nicklas et al., 2017.

claim: ATAD1 has been conserved over the 1 billion years of evolution separating yeast and humans.
source: This housekeeping role of ATAD1 is important for cellular health, as evidenced by the findings that ATAD1 is essential for life in mammals and has been conserved over the 1 billion years of evolution separating yeast and humans (Zhang et al., 2011; Ahrens-Nicklas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2011 and Ahrens-Nicklas et al., 2017.

claim: ATAD1 protein was undetectable in 21 of the 37 PTEN-null tumors analyzed.
source: ATAD1 protein was undetectable in 21 of the 37 PTEN-null tumors analyzed, but was present in all 15 PTEN-WT control tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: ATAD1 protein was present in all 15 PTEN-WT control tumors.
source: ATAD1 protein was undetectable in 21 of the 37 PTEN-null tumors analyzed, but was present in all 15 PTEN-WT control tumors (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: The majority of tumors harboring deep deletions in PTEN also had deep deletions in ATAD1.
source: Analysis of genomic data from The Cancer Genome Atlas corroborated these protein-level findings, as the majority of tumors harboring deep deletions in PTEN also had deep deletions in ATAD1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is based on TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: ATAD1 is almost never deleted in the absence of PTEN deletion.
source: Importantly, ATAD1 is almost never deleted in the absence of PTEN deletion (Figure 1B), nor does it feature recurrent inactivating point mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), which argues that ATAD1 is not a tumor suppressor.
evidence: This is based on TCGA data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: ATAD1 does not feature recurrent inactivating point mutations.
source: Importantly, ATAD1 is almost never deleted in the absence of PTEN deletion (Figure 1B), nor does it feature recurrent inactivating point mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), which argues that ATAD1 is not a tumor suppressor.
evidence: This is based on mutation data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: ATAD1 is not a tumor suppressor.
source: Importantly, ATAD1 is almost never deleted in the absence of PTEN deletion (Figure 1B), nor does it feature recurrent inactivating point mutations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E), which argues that ATAD1 is not a tumor suppressor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ATAD1 is only deleted with PTEN and lacks inactivating mutations.

claim: ATAD1 deletion is a 'hitchhiker' with the oncogenic driver deletion of PTEN.
source: Therefore, we hypothesize that ATAD1 deletion is simply a 'hitchhiker' with the oncogenic driver deletion of PTEN.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the co-deletion pattern observed in the data.

claim: PTEN deletions most frequently span the 0.5 Mb surrounding PTEN, leading to collateral deletion of KLLN and RNLS in addition to ATAD1.
source: These deletions most frequently span the 0.5 Mb surrounding PTEN, leading to collateral deletion of KLLN and RNLS in addition to ATAD1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on copy number variation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: ATAD1 is deleted in more than 25% of prostate cancer.
source: Altogether, ATAD1 is deleted at a high frequency across many tumor types, including in more than 25% of prostate cancer, 11% of melanoma, 7% of glioblastoma, and 4% of gastric adenocarcinoma (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ATAD1 is deleted in 11% of melanoma.
source: Altogether, ATAD1 is deleted at a high frequency across many tumor types, including in more than 25% of prostate cancer, 11% of melanoma, 7% of glioblastoma, and 4% of gastric adenocarcinoma (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ATAD1 is deleted in 7% of glioblastoma.
source: Altogether, ATAD1 is deleted at a high frequency across many tumor types, including in more than 25% of prostate cancer, 11% of melanoma, 7% of glioblastoma, and 4% of gastric adenocarcinoma (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ATAD1 is deleted in 4% of gastric adenocarcinoma.
source: Altogether, ATAD1 is deleted at a high frequency across many tumor types, including in more than 25% of prostate cancer, 11% of melanoma, 7% of glioblastoma, and 4% of gastric adenocarcinoma (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is based on data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MARCH5 was the top candidate for synthetic lethality with ATAD1 in the Jurkat CRISPR screen.
source: The top 10 candidates for ATAD1 synthetic lethality include five genes that encode mitochondrial proteins (MARCH5, TAZ, MTCH1, TOP3A, DNM1L) and two components of the ubiquitin proteasome system (MARCH5, PSMC6), which are both processes with clear relevance to the known functions of ATAD1 (Calvo et al., 2016; Figure 1E).
evidence: This is based on CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: MARCH5 is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes protein degradation on the OMM.
source: MARCH5 (also known as MITOL) was a particularly interesting hit, since it is an E3 ubiquitin ligase that promotes protein degradation on the OMM (Nakamura et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Nakamura et al., 2006.

claim: ATAD1 is deleted in 4.1% of gastric cancer.
source: ATAD1 is deleted in 4.1% of gastric cancer, a disease that causes nearly 800,000 deaths worldwide each year (Ferlay et al., 2019), therefore, we estimate that 32,000 patients die every year from ATAD1-deficient gastric cancer.
evidence: This is based on data analysis and a citation to Ferlay et al., 2019.

claim: Gastric cancer causes nearly 800,000 deaths worldwide each year.
source: ATAD1 is deleted in 4.1% of gastric cancer, a disease that causes nearly 800,000 deaths worldwide each year (Ferlay et al., 2019), therefore, we estimate that 32,000 patients die every year from ATAD1-deficient gastric cancer.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Ferlay et al., 2019.

claim: Approximately 32,000 patients die every year from ATAD1-deficient gastric cancer.
source: ATAD1 is deleted in 4.1% of gastric cancer, a disease that causes nearly 800,000 deaths worldwide each year (Ferlay et al., 2019), therefore, we estimate that 32,000 patients die every year from ATAD1-deficient gastric cancer.
evidence: This is calculated from the gastric cancer death rate and ATAD1 deletion frequency.

claim: MARCH5 was the top candidate for synthetic lethality with ATAD1 in the HGC27 CRISPR screen.
source: The top candidate for synthetic lethality with ATAD1 was MARCH5 (Figure 1G), a gene also identified in the Jurkat screen described above.
evidence: This is based on CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Deletion of MARCH5 had a negligible effect on fitness in ATAD1-proficient HGC27 cells.
source: Deletion of MARCH5 had a negligible effect on fitness in ATAD1-proficient HGC27 cells, but was an essential gene (by MAGeCK) in the EV cells (ATAD1-deficient).
evidence: This is based on CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MARCH5 was an essential gene in ATAD1-deficient HGC27 cells.
source: Deletion of MARCH5 had a negligible effect on fitness in ATAD1-proficient HGC27 cells, but was an essential gene (by MAGeCK) in the EV cells (ATAD1-deficient).
evidence: This is based on CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MUL1 was a top hit for synthetic lethality with ATAD1 in the HGC27 screen.
source: A second OMM-localized ubiquitin E3 ligase, MUL1, was also a top hit for synthetic lethality with ATAD1.
evidence: This is based on CRISPR screen data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: MARCH5 encodes a ubiquitin E3 ligase that ubiquitinates OMM proteins to trigger their extraction by p97/VCP and subsequent degradation by the proteasome.
source: Second, MARCH5 encodes a ubiquitin E3 ligase that ubiquitinates OMM proteins to trigger their extraction by p97/VCP and subsequent degradation by the proteasome (Nakamura et al., 2006; Cherok et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakamura et al., 2006 and Cherok et al., 2017.

claim: MARCH5/p97 and ATAD1 mediate two parallel pathways by which OMM proteins are removed from mitochondria.
source: MARCH5/p97 and ATAD1 mediate two parallel pathways by which OMM proteins are removed from mitochondria.
evidence: This is inferred from the known functions of MARCH5 and ATAD1 and their synthetic lethal interaction.

claim: The key function of MARCH5 is to suppress apoptosis.
source: It has recently become clear that the key function of MARCH5 is to suppress apoptosis (Djajawi et al., 2020; Haschka et al., 2020; Subramanian et al., 2016; Arai et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to four recent studies.

claim: Apoptosis is regulated by OMM-localized BCL2 family proteins and requires the permeabilization of the OMM by BAX/BAK.
source: Apoptosis is regulated by OMM-localized BCL2 family proteins and requires the permeabilization of the OMM by BAX/BAK (Kale et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kale et al., 2018 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Pro-survival proteins such as MCL1 bind to and inhibit BAX/BAK to prevent inappropriate cell death.
source: Pro-survival proteins such as MCL1 bind to and inhibit BAX/BAK to prevent inappropriate cell death (Greaves et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Greaves et al., 2019 and represents established knowledge.

claim: BH3-only proteins trigger apoptosis by binding and inhibiting pro-survival proteins like MCL1 and in some cases by directly activating BAX/BAK.
source: A variety of stressors activate BH3-only proteins (e.g. BIM), which trigger apoptosis by binding and inhibiting pro-survival proteins like MCL1 and in some cases by directly activating BAX/BAK (Letai, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Letai, 2017 and represents established knowledge.

claim: BH3-only proteins serve as sentinels for cellular stress and, upon activation, initiate mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization.
source: BH3-only proteins serve as sentinels for cellular stress and, upon activation, initiate mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (Bhatt et al., 2020; Llambi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bhatt et al., 2020 and Llambi et al., 2011.

claim: MARCH5 acts as a 'guardian' of MCL1 through an incompletely understood mechanism that involves the degradation of the pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins BIM and/or NOXA.
source: MARCH5 acts as a 'guardian' of MCL1 through an incompletely understood mechanism that involves the degradation of the pro-apoptotic BH3-only proteins BIM and/or NOXA (Kale et al., 2018; Letai, 2017; Llambi et al., 2011; Czabotar et al., 2014; Lin et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: BIM structurally resembles known substrates of ATAD1/Msp1 in that it is TA, has an intrinsically disordered region N-terminal to the transmembrane domain, and has basic residues at the extreme C-terminus.
source: Indeed, BIM structurally resembles known substrates of ATAD1/Msp1 in that it is TA, has an intrinsically disordered region N-terminal to the transmembrane domain, and has basic residues at the extreme C-terminus (Castanzo et al., 2020; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Castanzo et al., 2020 and Li et al., 2019.

claim: The abundance of BIMEL was increased in ATAD1∆ cells.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the abundance of BIMEL (the predominant isoform of BIM) was increased in ATAD1∆ cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Deletion of ATAD1 decreased BIMEL phosphorylation.
source: Deletion of ATAD1 decreased BIMEL phosphorylation, as assessed by decreased mobility in SDS-PAGE (Figure 2B), and with phospho-specific antibodies for residues Ser69 and Ser77 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATAD1 activity promoted the inhibitory phosphorylation of BIM at Ser69 and Ser77.
source: While ATAD1 activity promoted the inhibitory phosphorylation of BIM at Ser69 and Ser77, it did not affect BIM phosphorylation at Thr112, a phosphorylation site that potentiates the pro-death activity of BIM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATAD1 did not affect BIM phosphorylation at Thr112.
source: While ATAD1 activity promoted the inhibitory phosphorylation of BIM at Ser69 and Ser77, it did not affect BIM phosphorylation at Thr112, a phosphorylation site that potentiates the pro-death activity of BIM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of ATAD1 increased BIM levels.
source: Deletion of ATAD1 increased BIM levels, while deletion of MARCH5 increased NOXA levels (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of MARCH5 increased NOXA levels.
source: Deletion of ATAD1 increased BIM levels, while deletion of MARCH5 increased NOXA levels (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of both MARCH5 and ATAD1 increased the abundance of both NOXA and BIM.
source: Accordingly, deletion of both MARCH5 and ATAD1 increased the abundance of both NOXA and BIM, which work together to antagonize the pro-survival protein MCL1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Deletion of MARCH5 caused a modest decrease in viability in WT Jurkat cells.
source: Deletion of MARCH5 caused a modest decrease in viability in WT Jurkat cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: ATAD1∆ cells were hypersensitive to MARCH5 deletion.
source: ATAD1∆ cells, however, were hypersensitive to MARCH5 deletion, as expected from our CRISPR screen results.
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: BIM knockout partially rescued the hypersensitivity of ATAD1∆ cells to MARCH5 deletion.
source: Interestingly, BIM knockout partially rescued the hypersensitivity of ATAD1∆ cells to MARCH5 deletion (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The synthetic lethal interaction of ATAD1 and MARCH5 was suppressed in cells stably overexpressing MCL1.
source: Indeed, we found that the synthetic lethal interaction of ATAD1 and MARCH5 was suppressed in cells stably overexpressing MCL1 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: ATAD1∆ cells were hypersensitive to intermediate expression of ectopic BIMEL.
source: However, ATAD1∆ cells were hypersensitive to intermediate expression of ectopic BIMEL, as measured by cell viability assays (Figure 2G), cleaved PARP immunoblots (Figure 2F), and live cell imaging using the Incucyte platform (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is based on multiple assays shown in Figure 2F, 2G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Endogenous ATAD1 protects against BIM but ATAD1 can be overwhelmed with sufficiently high levels of BIM.
source: Thus, endogenous ATAD1 protects against BIM but ATAD1 can be overwhelmed with sufficiently high levels of BIM.
evidence: This is inferred from the dose-dependent effects of BIM expression shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: BIM is sufficient to induce apoptosis preferentially in cells lacking ATAD1.
source: These results demonstrate that BIM is sufficient to induce apoptosis preferentially in cells lacking ATAD1.
evidence: This is based on the BIM overexpression experiments shown in Figure 2F-G.

claim: H4 glioma cells were highly sensitive to BIM peptide, which is rescued by re-expression of ATAD1WT but not the catalytically dead ATAD1E193Q mutant.
source: H4 glioma cells (Del(10q23); ATAD1-null; Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) were highly sensitive to BIM peptide, which is rescued by re-expression of ATAD1WT but not the catalytically dead ATAD1E193Q mutant (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is based on BH3 profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: ATAD1 suppresses overall apoptotic priming, as measured by sensitivity to BIM BH3 peptide.
source: ATAD1 therefore appears to suppress overall apoptotic priming, at least in this context, as measured by sensitivity to BIM BH3 peptide.
evidence: This is inferred from the BH3 profiling data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: GFP-BIMEL co-immunoprecipitated with FLAG-tagged ATAD1 in H4 cells.
source: Consistent with BIM being an ATAD1 substrate, GFP-BIMEL co-immunoprecipitated with FLAG-tagged ATAD1 in H4 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: ATAD1-FLAG co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous BIM.
source: Inversely, ATAD1-FLAG co-immunoprecipitated with endogenous BIM (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is based on co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E.

claim: ATAD1 and BIM physically interact in cells.
source: Thus, reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation argues that ATAD1 and BIM physically interact in cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: His6-ATAD1 directly and efficiently extracted 3xFLAG-BIML from liposomes.
source: His6-ATAD1 directly and efficiently extracted 3xFLAG-BIML from liposomes in this assay (Figure 2I; compare lanes with elution 'E' to input 'I'; lanes 13–16).
evidence: This is based on in vitro extraction assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ATAD1 extraction of BIM was ATP-dependent.
source: As expected, this activity was ATP-dependent (Figure 2I, lanes 17–20) and was abolished when we used the catalytically inactive mutant, ATAD1E193Q (Figure 2I, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is based on in vitro extraction assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ATAD1 extraction of BIM was abolished when using the catalytically inactive mutant ATAD1E193Q.
source: As expected, this activity was ATP-dependent (Figure 2I, lanes 17–20) and was abolished when we used the catalytically inactive mutant, ATAD1E193Q (Figure 2I, lanes 1–4).
evidence: This is based on in vitro extraction assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ATAD1 requires membrane anchoring for its dislocase activity.
source: Omission of Ni-chelating lipids from the liposomes ('Mito Lipos', which cannot anchor His6-ATAD1; Figure 2I, lanes 5–8) prevented ATAD1 from extracting BIM, demonstrating that ATAD1 requires membrane anchoring for its dislocase activity.
evidence: This is based on in vitro extraction assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: ATAD1 did not extract yeast Fis1.
source: Importantly, ATAD1 did not extract yeast Fis1, consistent with previous reports that Fis1 is not an Msp1 substrate (Li et al., 2019; Figure 2I, lanes 9–12).
evidence: This is based on in vitro extraction assay data shown in Figure 2I and is consistent with prior work.

claim: ATAD1 extracted BIM in an ATP-dependent manner but failed to extract BIK or PUMA under the same conditions.
source: ATAD1 extracted BIM in an ATP-dependent manner, as expected, but failed to extract BIK or PUMA under the same conditions (Figure 2J and K).
evidence: This is based on in vitro extraction assay data shown in Figure 2J and K.

claim: BIM differs from BIK and PUMA in that it has a positively charged C-terminus and an intrinsically disordered region N-terminal to the transmembrane domain.
source: While it is not clear how ATAD1 distinguishes between these substrates, BIM differs from BIK and PUMA in that it has a positively charged C-terminus and an intrinsically disordered region N-terminal to the transmembrane domain, which are important features for substrate recognition by Msp1, the yeast homolog of ATAD1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5; Castanzo et al., 2020; Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5 and citations to prior work.

claim: ATAD1 altered the localization of BIM under basal conditions, generating GFP-positive puncta that did not colocalize with mitochondria.
source: ATAD1 altered the localization of BIM under basal conditions, generating GFP-positive puncta that did not colocalize with mitochondria (Figure 2—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6A.

claim: Treatment with bortezomib exacerbated the phenotype of ATAD1-induced BIM puncta and resulted in larger, brighter GFP-positive puncta only in ATAD1 expressing cells.
source: Treatment with bortezomib exacerbated this phenotype and resulted in larger, brighter GFP-positive puncta only in ATAD1 expressing cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 6B and C).
evidence: This is based on confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6B and C.

claim: Bortezomib treatment led to the accumulation of phosphorylated BIMEL in SW1088 cells expressing ATAD1.
source: Bortezomib treatment led to the accumulation of phosphorylated BIMEL in SW1088 cells expressing ATAD1, while BIMEL accumulated in an unphosphorylated state in SW1088 cells transduced with EV (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: BIM accumulated in a phosphorylated state after treatment with bortezomib in PC3 cells with ATAD1 present.
source: In parallel to our findings with SW1088 cells, BIM accumulated in a phosphorylated state after treatment with bortezomib in PC3 cells with ATAD1 present (sgNT), but this phosphorylation was abrogated in PC3 cells with ATAD1 deleted (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: In the context of proteasome inhibition, ATAD1 shifts the localization of BIM from mitochondria to cytoplasmic puncta and promotes inhibitory phosphorylation of BIM.
source: Thus, in the context of proteasome inhibition, ATAD1 shifts the localization of BIM from mitochondria to cytoplasmic puncta and promotes inhibitory phosphorylation of BIM.
evidence: This is inferred from the microscopy and western blot data showing BIM localization and phosphorylation changes.

claim: Re-expression of ATAD1 in Del(10q23) cell lines suppressed toxicity caused by various structurally distinct proteasome inhibitors.
source: Re-expression of ATAD1 in the Del(10q23) cell lines HGC27 (gastric cancer), SW1088 (glioma), or RPMI7951 (melanoma) suppressed toxicity caused by various structurally distinct proteasome inhibitors (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 3A-C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: Deletion of ATAD1 increased sensitivity to bortezomib in PC3 cells.
source: Deletion of ATAD1 increased sensitivity to bortezomib in PC3 cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Overexpressing ATAD1WT, but not ATAD1E193Q, made PC3 cells more resistant to bortezomib.
source: Inversely, overexpressing ATAD1WT, but not ATAD1E193Q, made PC3 cells more resistant to bortezomib (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Bortezomib treatment induced robust PARP cleavage in ATAD1-deficient cells but not in cognate ATAD1-positive cells.
source: Indeed, bortezomib treatment induced robust PARP cleavage in the same ATAD1-deficient cells described above, but not in cognate ATAD1-positive cells (Figure 3E–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 3E-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-C.

claim: Bortezomib treatment caused polyubiquitinated proteins to accumulate to the same extent in the presence or absence of ATAD1.
source: Bortezomib treatment caused polyubiquitinated proteins to accumulate to the same extent in the presence or absence of ATAD1, indicating that ATAD1 affects how the cell responds to proteotoxic stress, rather than blocking the proteotoxic insult itself (Figure 3E–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is based on western blot data shown in Figure 3E-G and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: ATAD1 affects how the cell responds to proteotoxic stress, rather than blocking the proteotoxic insult itself.
source: Bortezomib treatment caused polyubiquitinated proteins to accumulate to the same extent in the presence or absence of ATAD1, indicating that ATAD1 affects how the cell responds to proteotoxic stress, rather than blocking the proteotoxic insult itself (Figure 3E–G, Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that polyubiquitinated proteins accumulate equally regardless of ATAD1 status.

claim: ATAD1 is essential for viability in cells subjected to ubiquitin proteasome system dysfunction.
source: Thus, ATAD1 appears to be essential for viability in cells subjected to ubiquitin proteasome system dysfunction.
evidence: This is inferred from the viability and apoptosis data showing ATAD1-deficient cells are hypersensitive to proteasome inhibition.

claim: Treatment of ATAD1 knockout PC3 cells with the caspase inhibitor zVAD-FMK rescued the effects of bortezomib essentially back to WT levels.
source: Treatment of ATAD1 knockout PC3 cells with the caspase inhibitor zVAD-FMK rescued the effects of bortezomib essentially back to WT levels (Figure 3H; Figure 3—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3E.

claim: ATAD1 re-expression phenocopied treatment with zVAD-fmk in RPMI7951 cells treated with bortezomib.
source: Additionally, ATAD1 re-expression phenocopied treatment with zVAD-fmk in RPMI7951 cells (Del(10q23)) treated with bortezomib (Figure 3—figure supplement 3F and G).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3F and G.

claim: There was no additive effect of zVAD-fmk and ATAD1, suggesting that ATAD1 and zVAD-fmk act in a linear pathway to prevent the death of cells subjected to proteasome inhibition.
source: Moreover, there was no additive effect of zVAD-fmk and ATAD1, suggesting that ATAD1 and zVAD-fmk act in a linear pathway to prevent the death of cells subjected to proteasome inhibition (Figure 3H, Figure 3—figure supplement 3G and H).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of additive effects shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3G and H.

claim: Caspase inhibition completely rescued the bortezomib phenotype of ATAD1-deficient cells.
source: Although caspase inhibition completely rescued the bortezomib phenotype of ATAD1-deficient cells, the same was not true for deletion of BIM in PC3 cells, implying that other factors in addition to BIM mediate this phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Deletion of BIM did not completely rescue the bortezomib phenotype of ATAD1-deficient cells, implying that other factors in addition to BIM mediate this phenotype.
source: Although caspase inhibition completely rescued the bortezomib phenotype of ATAD1-deficient cells, the same was not true for deletion of BIM in PC3 cells, implying that other factors in addition to BIM mediate this phenotype (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B).
evidence: This is based on viability assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B.

claim: The protective effects of ATAD1 during proteasome inhibition can be explained exclusively by limiting apoptosis, with BIM extraction playing a key role.
source: Nonetheless, these results indicate that the protective effects of ATAD1 during proteasome inhibition can be explained exclusively by limiting apoptosis, with BIM extraction playing a key role.
evidence: This is inferred from the caspase inhibition and BIM deletion experiments.

claim: Bortezomib significantly decreased the growth rate of PC3 tumors in which ATAD1 was deleted.
source: Bortezomib had no effect on growth of PC3 xenografts transduced with sgNT, but significantly decreased the growth rate of tumors in which ATAD1 was deleted (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is based on xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Bortezomib had no effect on growth of PC3 xenografts transduced with sgNT.
source: Bortezomib had no effect on growth of PC3 xenografts transduced with sgNT, but significantly decreased the growth rate of tumors in which ATAD1 was deleted (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is based on xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: Bortezomib treatment induced a significant increase in NOXA levels in sgATAD1 tumors, but not in sgNT tumors.
source: Bortezomib treatment induced a significant increase in NOXA levels in sgATAD1 tumors, but not in sgNT tumors (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on western blot data from tumor samples shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NRF1 was equally induced by bortezomib in sgNT and sgATAD1 tumors.
source: NRF1 was equally induced by bortezomib in sgNT and sgATAD1 tumors (Figure 4C; Figure 4—figure supplement 1), again supporting our conclusion that ATAD1 protects cells from death triggered by protein stress rather than preventing the protein stress itself.
evidence: This is based on western blot data from tumor samples shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Bortezomib is preferentially toxic to PC3 tumors that lack ATAD1.
source: Altogether, these in vivo results demonstrate that bortezomib is preferentially toxic to PC3 tumors that lack ATAD1.
evidence: This is inferred from the xenograft tumor growth data shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: ATAD1 was not necessary for basal tumor growth in PC3 cells.
source: ATAD1 was not necessary for basal tumor growth in PC3 cells, so we assessed the effect of ATAD1 on tumor growth of SW1088 cells, a Del(10q23) glioma cell line that is non-tumorigenic in SCID mice (Jiang et al., 2017; Mercapide et al., 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the xenograft data and is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: SW1088 cells transduced with EV failed to form tumors in 17 out of 17 NOD/SCID mice.
source: As expected, SW1088 cells transduced with EV failed to form tumors in 17 out of 17 NOD/SCID mice.
evidence: This is based on xenograft data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: SW1088 cells transduced with ATAD1 grew palpable tumors in 20 out of 21 mice.
source: However, SW1088 cells transduced with ATAD1 grew palpable tumors in 20 out of 21 mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on xenograft data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: ATAD1 promotes growth of SW1088 glioma xenografts.
source: ATAD1 thus promotes growth of SW1088 glioma xenografts, despite not affecting their proliferation in 2D culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on xenograft data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-B and cell culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: ATAD1 does not affect SW1088 cell proliferation in 2D culture.
source: ATAD1 thus promotes growth of SW1088 glioma xenografts, despite not affecting their proliferation in 2D culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is based on cell culture data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The median overall survival of mCRPC patients with PTEN-null ATAD1-null tumors (77 months) was more than double that of patients with only PTEN-null or 'unaltered' tumors (37 months).
source: The median overall survival of mCRPC patients with PTEN-null ATAD1-null tumors (77 months) was more than double that of patients with only PTEN-null or 'unaltered' tumors (37 months, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on patient survival data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Patients whose tumors lacked both ATAD1 and PTEN had longer survival post-therapy than did the patients whose tumors lacked only PTEN.
source: In a subset of patients, we were able to additionally assess overall survival after initial hormone therapy or chemotherapy. Patients whose tumors lacked both ATAD1 and PTEN had longer survival post-therapy than did the patients whose tumors lacked only PTEN (Figure 4E and F).
evidence: This is based on patient survival data shown in Figure 4E and F.

claim: ATAD1 exerts a pro-survival effect in tumor cells in both murine xenografts and human mCRPC patients.
source: Altogether, these data suggest that ATAD1 exerts a pro-survival effect in tumor cells (with ATAD1 deficiency decreasing tumor fitness and improving patient survival) in both murine xenografts and human mCRPC patients.
evidence: This is inferred from the xenograft and patient survival data.

claim: Co-deletion of PTEN likely buffers some of the apoptotic priming induced by ATAD1 loss.
source: This may be partly explained by the strong selection for deletion of PTEN, which virtually always co-occurs with deletion of ATAD1. PTEN loss activates AKT, which has pro-survival effects, including decreasing transcription of BCL2L11 (BIM) by inhibiting FOXO3A, and inactivating the BH3-only protein BAD by direct phosphorylation (Gilley et al., 2003; Datta et al., 1997). Therefore, co-deletion of PTEN likely buffers some of the apoptotic priming induced by ATAD1 loss.
evidence: This is inferred from known functions of PTEN and AKT, supported by citations.

claim: PTEN loss activates AKT, which has pro-survival effects, including decreasing transcription of BCL2L11 (BIM) by inhibiting FOXO3A, and inactivating the BH3-only protein BAD by direct phosphorylation.
source: PTEN loss activates AKT, which has pro-survival effects, including decreasing transcription of BCL2L11 (BIM) by inhibiting FOXO3A, and inactivating the BH3-only protein BAD by direct phosphorylation (Gilley et al., 2003; Datta et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gilley et al., 2003 and Datta et al., 1997.

claim: Genetic lesions that prime cells for apoptosis are not always selected against in cancer.
source: Furthermore, genetic lesions that prime cells for apoptosis are not always selected against in cancer.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: Certain oncogenes (including MYC paralogs) are strongly selected for, despite their known effect of priming for apoptosis.
source: On the contrary, certain oncogenes (including MYC paralogs) are strongly selected for, despite their known effect of priming for apoptosis (Mason et al., 2008; Dammert et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mason et al., 2008 and Dammert et al., 2019.

claim: ATAD1 is particularly important for cellular health in the context of ubiquitin proteasome system dysfunction.
source: These data also illustrate that ATAD1 is particularly important for cellular health in the context of ubiquitin proteasome system dysfunction, which can be at least partly explained by ATAD1 antagonizing BIM.
evidence: This is inferred from the proteasome inhibitor sensitivity data.

claim: Patients with metastatic prostate cancer tumors that lack ATAD1 live significantly longer.
source: Patients with metastatic prostate cancer tumors that lack ATAD1 live significantly longer, and appear to respond better to therapy, which suggests that ATAD1 is also important in the context of human tumors subjected to different stressors.
evidence: This is based on patient survival data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Patients with metastatic prostate cancer tumors that lack ATAD1 appear to respond better to therapy.
source: Patients with metastatic prostate cancer tumors that lack ATAD1 live significantly longer, and appear to respond better to therapy, which suggests that ATAD1 is also important in the context of human tumors subjected to different stressors.
evidence: This is based on patient survival data shown in Figure 4E-F.

claim: ATAD1 was originally discovered in mammals via a genetic screen for factors that prevent neuronal cell death.
source: ATAD1 has not been explicitly linked to apoptosis, but it was originally discovered in mammals via a genetic screen for factors that prevent neuronal cell death (Dai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dai et al., 2010.

claim: Atad1 phenocopies Bcl2 and Bcl2l1 in the middle cerebral artery occlusion mouse model of ischemic stroke: deletion of Atad1 or Bcl2 exacerbates, and overexpression of Atad1, Bcl2, or Bcl2l1 decreases ischemic cell death.
source: Further, Atad1 phenocopies Bcl2 and Bcl2l1 in the middle cerebral artery occlusion mouse model of ischemic stroke: deletion of Atad1 or Bcl2 exacerbates, and overexpression of Atad1, Bcl2, or Bcl2l1 decreases ischemic cell death (Zhang et al., 2019; Martinou et al., 1994; Parsadanian et al., 1998; Broughton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple prior studies.

claim: Antagonism of BIM may contribute to the neuroprotective function of ATAD1 in vivo.
source: We speculate that antagonism of BIM may contribute to the neuroprotective function of ATAD1 in vivo (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings in this study and prior work.

claim: Deletion of BIM does not completely rescue the effects of ATAD1.
source: One limitation of our study is that deletion of BIM does not completely rescue the effects of ATAD1.
evidence: This is based on the genetic interaction experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4A.

claim: There must be other ATAD1 substrates that contribute to the proteasome inhibition phenotype of ATAD1-null cells.
source: Even though we demonstrate that BIM is an ATAD1 substrate and that this interaction is important for the pro-survival effects of ATAD1 (such as the synthetic lethality of ATAD1 and MARCH5), there must be other ATAD1 substrates that contribute to the proteasome inhibition phenotype of ATAD1-null cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the incomplete rescue by BIM deletion.

claim: A multitude of ATAD1 substrates accumulate on the OMM during proteasome inhibition, and deletion of a single one (e.g. BIM) is insufficient to counteract the summative stress.
source: We speculate that a multitude of ATAD1 substrates accumulate on the OMM during proteasome inhibition, and deletion of a single one (e.g. BIM) is insufficient to counteract the summative stress.
evidence: This is speculation based on the incomplete rescue by BIM deletion.

claim: Cells lacking ATAD1 have an increased dependency on the ubiquitin proteasome system.
source: Overall, these data show that cells lacking ATAD1 have an increased dependency on the ubiquitin proteasome system.
evidence: This is inferred from the synthetic lethality with MARCH5 and proteasome inhibitor sensitivity.

claim: Mitochondrial TA proteins have (at least) two fates: extraction by ATAD1, and ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: We therefore propose a model in which mitochondrial TA proteins have (at least) two fates: extraction by ATAD1, and ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the findings in this study, illustrated in Figure 4G.

claim: ATAD1 becomes important for cellular viability only in the context of a dysfunctional UPS.
source: This model is strongly supported by the finding that ATAD1 becomes important for cellular viability only in the context of a dysfunctional UPS, such as upon MARCH5 deletion or pharmacological inhibition of the proteasome.
evidence: This is based on the synthetic lethality and proteasome inhibitor sensitivity data.

claim: Caspase inhibition completely rescues the absence of ATAD1 in proteasome inhibitor treated cells, arguing that ATAD1 is important in this context specifically for preventing apoptosis.
source: That caspase inhibition completely rescues the absence of ATAD1 in proteasome inhibitor treated cells argues that ATAD1 is important in this context specifically for preventing apoptosis, as opposed to a general loss of cell fitness.
evidence: This is based on the caspase inhibition experiments shown in Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: ATAD1 loss sensitizes to proteasome dysfunction could have therapeutic implications for hundreds of thousands of cancer patients with Del(10q23) tumors.
source: That ATAD1 loss sensitizes to proteasome dysfunction could have therapeutic implications for hundreds of thousands of cancer patients with Del(10q23) tumors, especially considering that drugs targeting the proteasome are already approved for the treatment of cancer.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic applications based on the findings.

claim: Previous trials of proteasome inhibitors in unselected patients with prostate cancer have shown activity in a subset of patients.
source: Previous trials of proteasome inhibitors in unselected patients with prostate cancer have shown activity in a subset of patients, consistent with the possibility that this subset was enriched for patients with ATAD1-null tumors (Papandreou et al., 2004; Naik et al., 2018; Morris et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical trials.

claim: Pharmacological inhibitors of MARCH5 could achieve an even better therapeutic window than proteasome inhibitors in treating tumors with ATAD1 deletion.
source: We predict that pharmacological inhibitors of MARCH5 could achieve an even better therapeutic window than proteasome inhibitors in treating tumors with ATAD1 deletion, and would be an exciting area for drug development.
evidence: This is speculation about potential therapeutic strategies based on the findings.
